title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
gist: A Quilty Space report finds that outside China there will be about 150 fewer launches than demand through 2030, a crunch more severe than expected and lasting possibly to the late 2030s. SpaceX's Falcon 9 wind-down and Starship's lack of a conventional fairing are central uncertainties.

themes.theme: Scale and duration of the shortage

insights.claim: Quilty Space estimates a shortfall of about 150 launches through 2030 relative to demand from satellite operators and civil agencies outside China, and it could double if military demand is added and Falcon is not extended.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Launch scarcity should support pricing power and backlog value for providers with capacity.

insights.claim: Quilty's Caleb Henry says the crisis is more severe than thought, will not end this decade, and might not abate until the late 2030s, with the crunch most acute in 2028.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Satellite operators without booked launches face delays; 'if you haven't booked your launch already, you're late'.
insights.quote: the launch crisis is more severe than we thought

insights.claim: Drivers include the Ukraine war removing Russian rockets from Western markets, Amazon Leo demand, delays in New Glenn, Vulcan, Neutron, Terran R and Nova, and the retirement of Falcon 9 for commercial service.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Supply is contracting while demand soars.
insights.locator: The report tallies a number of familiar factors

insights.claim: SpaceX has intensified the shortage by winding down Falcon 9 and has stopped affirming Starship as a commercial launcher, per the Quilty report.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Starship will not relieve the crunch soon for third-party customers.
insights.quote: SpaceX has also stopped affirming Starship as a commercial launcher
insights.locator: Starship's lack of a regular fairing

insights.claim: There is no evidence SpaceX is developing a conventional payload fairing door for Starship, which keeps its narrow Starlink-style dispenser, so customers may need flat satellites.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Satellite designs may have to adapt to Starship dispensers.
insights.locator: Starship's lack of a regular fairing

insights.claim: Telesat CEO Dan Goldberg expects SpaceX to prioritize its own satellites and US government, with Telesat access depending on its satellites fitting SpaceX's dispenser.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Commercial Starship access is conditional and secondary.
insights.locator: Starship's lack of a regular fairing

themes.theme: Wildcards: Blue Origin and military demand

insights.claim: Quilty's conservative forecast has Blue Origin flying eight New Glenn launches in 2028, 12 in 2029 and 16 in 2030, while Blue builds capacity for up to 150 upper stages annually.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Faster New Glenn ramp is the main upside risk to the shortage thesis.
insights.locator: What about Blue and Uncle Sam?

insights.claim: The Space Force raised forecast demand for Lane 1 from 30-60 launches to about 170 and for Lane 2 from 54 to 79, for missions ordered 2025-2029, which Quilty excluded from its base case.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Military demand could crowd out commercial customers.
insights.locator: What about Blue and Uncle Sam?

insights.claim: Henry expects the US government to compel SpaceX to perform national priority launches, noting SpaceX is already building many such satellites, such as the SB-AMTI constellation.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Government priority could further tighten commercial availability.
insights.quote: I think the US government will compel them to do this
insights.locator: What about Blue and Uncle Sam?
